newsitem.title: MEXICO: Mexico stocks slide at close on U.S. Senate vote.
newsitem.headline: Mexico stocks slide at close on U.S. Senate vote.

text.p: Mexican stocks extended their midday slump sharply at the close of trade on Thursday following news of a U.S. Senate vote to rebuke Mexico as a drugs war ally, traders said.

"This (the vote) hit the bourse because, although it was not outright decertification, it still makes dealers nervous. We started to slide faster once the news broke as they used it as a pretext to step up profit-taking" a floor trader said.
The leading IPC share index ended down 57.30 points, or 1.48 percent, at 3,809.90.
Key U.S. senators drafted a resolution that stopped short of proposing decertification, but would still criticize Mexico's drug-fighting efforts.
Traders remarked on the sharp drop posted by telecomms firm Telmex in both New York and Mexico, but offered different interpretations.
Telmex L shares plunged 78 centavos to 15.80 pesos, while its ADRs ended off two dollars at 39-5/8.
"The market was weighed down again by Telmex. It broke through the 41-mark yesterday, met with resistance and that's where sellers stepped in," the floor trader added.
Telmex L class accounted for almost one-quarter of all shares traded.
Nonetheless, other traders noted Telmex fell further than other ADRs listed on Wall Street and suggested the real reason it fell lay elsewhere.
"A lot of options fall due tomorrow and many are short on calls that strike at 40, so that may be a motive for hitting Telmex so hard," a Mexico City desk trader said.
ADRs listed by construction firm ICA fell 1/4 to 16-1/8 while conglomerate Desc actually gained 1/4 to 26-3/4.
The Dow Jones itself declined to a lesser extent than the IPC, by 0.83 percent to 6,820.28 points.
The trading volume scoreboard chalked up an unheard-of 1.072 billion shares traded, or some ten times that posted during an average session.

Dealers noted that four last-minute cross trades accounted for 981.4 million of nominal total volume. The trades were in A and B class shares listed by cable manufacturer Latinca, as part of a deal whereby Condumex, part of the Carso group, acquired the company.

Analysts said the bourse slumped for most of the session on expectations of a rise in U.S. interest rates at the March 25 Federal Open Market Committee meeting, prompted by congressional testimony from Federal Reserve Chairman Alan Greenspan.

"Greenspan's statements changed the outlook for next week and paved the way for changes. The problem is not that they might go up next week, but that there are signs they will do so over the coming months," said Leonor Gonzaalez, an equity analyst with the BBV-Probursa brokerage in Mexico City.
"The short-term impact will be negative once the FOMC move is announced, but the mexican bourse has been strong so the downturn may not be so drastic," she added.
On the broad market, meanwhile, 107 stocks changed hands, of which declines outnumbered gaines by 45 to 27.
Latincasa A and B shares topped the gaines list, which both climbed 20 centavos to 50 centavos.
Dealers noted financial groups were among the prominent sliders on a combination of profit-taking and fears of a forthcoming hike in U.S. interest rates.
((--Karina Balderas, Mexico City newsroom +525 728-7907))
